q: Commercial lumber in the Philippines is usually sold in what kind of lengths?
n: Commercial lumber is stocked in even-numbered lengths of feet (8', 10', 12'...). Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (lumber).

q: Where is coco lumber least commonly used?
n: Coco lumber is hard, fibrous and splits, so it is difficult to mill into the fine, accurate profiles of door jambs. It is used for forms, trusses and furniture. Source: PCA (Philippine Coconut Authority) coco lumber guidelines.

q: What is the main reason for seasoning lumber before use?
o: To reduce moisture content and prevent warping
n: Seasoning dries lumber to near its service moisture content, so it shrinks, warps and checks before use rather than in the building, and becomes stronger and decay-resistant. Source: US Forest Service, Wood Handbook (drying of wood).

q: How many board feet are in 250 pieces of 2" × 3" × 10' lumber?
n: Board feet = (thickness in. × width in. × length ft) ÷ 12. 2 × 3 × 10 ÷ 12 = 5 bd ft per piece, and 250 × 5 = 1,250 bd ft. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (lumber).

q: What is the general term for baseboards, cornices, balusters and similar detailed wood elements?
n: Millwork is wood products made in a planing mill: moldings, baseboards, cornices, balusters, doors, cabinets. Source: Architectural Woodwork Institute (AWI) Standards; Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which of these is NOT millwork?
n: Millwork is milled wood. Steel railings are metalwork, so they are not millwork. Source: AWI Standards.

q: Which item in this list is NOT millwork?
n: Light reflectors are lighting fixture parts, not milled woodwork, so they are not millwork. Source: AWI Standards.

q: Which of these is millwork?
n: A wood cornice is milled molding, so it is millwork. Millwork covers factory-milled wood items such as mouldings, trim, doors, frames and cornices, as opposed to rough framing lumber. Source: AWI Standards.

q: Which item in this list counts as millwork?
n: A wood dresser is fabricated in a mill shop, so it counts as millwork (casework). Steel handles, GI gutters and stainless railings are metal. Source: AWI Standards.

q: What connector joins members in wood trusses?
n: Gusset plates (plywood or steel) are nailed, bolted or glued across truss joints to connect the members. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood trusses); TPI 1 (truss design).

q: Where are gang nails typically used?
n: Gang nails (toothed metal connector plates) are pressed into both faces of joints in prefabricated wood trusses. Source: TPI 1 (metal plate connected wood trusses).

q: What adhesive is used to stick a wood board to concrete?
n: Construction adhesive, sold under brands like Liquid Nails, bonds wood boards and furring to concrete and masonry. Source: ASTM D3498 (adhesives for field-gluing); manufacturer literature.

q: Why must a board be positioned accurately when using liquid nail?
o: It is hard to correct once it has dried
n: Construction adhesive grabs quickly and is hard to break once cured, so a board must be positioned accurately the first time. Source: Construction adhesive manufacturer literature.

q: How would you install 3/4" plywood over an uneven surface?
n: Over an uneven surface, a leveled frame (angle bar or wood furring shimmed true) is installed first and the 3/4" plywood is fixed to it. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (furring).

q: What is the vernacular term for a wood joist?
n: Soleras is the Filipino carpentry term (from Spanish) for floor joists. Source: Filipino construction trade terminology.

q: What is the vernacular term for a rabbet joint?
n: Vaciada is the Filipino carpentry term for a rabbet, the L-shaped recess cut along a board edge. Source: Filipino construction trade terminology.

q: What tool is used to turn a baluster?
n: A torno is a lathe (from Spanish torno). Balusters are turned on it. Source: Filipino construction trade terminology.

q: What is the vernacular term for the wood molding at the bottom of a wall?
n: Rodapis is the Filipino trade term for the baseboard at the bottom of a wall. Source: Filipino construction trade terminology.

q: What is the vernacular term for the horizontal member at the top or bottom of a wall frame?
n: Tabla madre is the Filipino carpentry term for the main horizontal plate at the top or bottom of a wall frame. Source: Filipino construction trade terminology.

q: What is the structural support of a stair called?
n: The stringer (string) is the inclined structural member that supports the treads and risers of a stair. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (stairs).

q: What is the last part of a staircase?
n: A flight ends at a landing, the platform at the top (or between flights) where the stair run finishes. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (stairs).

q: What marks the starting point of a staircase?
n: A staircase starts at the first tread (starting step) at the bottom of the flight. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (stairs).

q: What post is located at the end of a stair run and anchors the handrail?
n: The newel post stands at the start, end and turns of a stair run and anchors the handrail. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (stairs).

q: What is the vertical part between two treads?
n: The riser is the vertical face between two treads. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (stairs); NBC IRR Rule XII.

q: What is the most suitable joint for wood flooring?
n: Wood strip flooring is tongue-and-groove, so the boards interlock, stay flush and can be blind-nailed through the tongue. Source: NWFA Installation Guidelines.

q: What type of joinery is commonly used for plywood connections?
n: Plywood panels are commonly joined with dado joints (grooves cut to receive the other panel), giving glue area and alignment in cabinets and shelving. Source: AWI Standards; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which joint is typically used for the back panel of a cabinet?
n: A cabinet back panel sits in a rabbet cut along the back edges of the carcass, hiding its edge and squaring the box. Source: AWI Standards (casework construction).

q: Which joint is commonly used at countertop corners?
n: Countertop corners are mitered (cut at 45° and joined) so the edge profile and laminate pattern continue around the corner. Source: AWI Standards (countertops).

q: Which joint gives interlocking strength and is often used at drawer corners?
n: Dovetails interlock mechanically and resist the pull on drawer fronts, the traditional strongest drawer-corner joint. Source: AWI Standards (drawer construction).

q: What do you call a light circular saw on a spring-loaded pivoting arm over a metal base?
n: A chop (miter) saw is a circular saw on a spring-loaded arm that pivots down onto work on a metal base, for accurate crosscuts and miters. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: Which power tool shapes and finishes wood with a continuous abrasive loop?
n: A belt sander drives a continuous abrasive loop over rollers to shape and smooth wood quickly. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: Which saw uses a reciprocating blade to cut irregular curves?
n: A jigsaw has a narrow reciprocating blade, so it can cut irregular curves and cutouts. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: Which saw cuts various materials and can be either handheld or table-mounted?
n: The circular saw is made both as a handheld tool and table- or arm-mounted, and cuts wood, metal or masonry with the right blade. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: What is a circular saw mounted under a table, with the work pushed across it?
n: A table saw has a circular blade projecting through a flat table, and the work is pushed across it for rip and crosscuts. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.
